cases.title: Same planet, four atmospheres
cases.mini: One observer, four horizontal rays that differ only in how strongly the air bends them. Ordinary air bends light a little. Only k = 1, a rare duct, bends it as much as the ground curves.
cases.text: One observer and four horizontal rays, differing only in the refraction coefficient k, the ratio of the ray's curvature to the Earth's. Over hot ground, k = −1 and light bends upward. In a vacuum, k = 0 and it goes straight. Standard air gives about k = 0.17, a ray curving at a sixth of the Earth's rate. At k = 1, the ray curves exactly as the ground does: there is no horizon, and the Earth would look flat. That happens only in ducts, thin layers of strong inversion over cold water or ice, and they announce themselves with stacked and inverted images and a slot-shaped Sun [1][2]. Curvature is exaggerated by the factor printed on the image; the ratios between the arcs are exact.
cases.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: k = 1 everywhere and always, not only in thin inversions that distort what they carry.
arc.title: A bent ray over a round Earth, or a straight ray over a bigger one
arc.mini: Light in ordinary air follows an arc of radius ρ = R/k. Bending the ray and the ground together, one can instead draw a straight ray over a larger Earth of radius R/(1 − k): the same geometry.
arc.text: In air whose density falls steadily with height, a nearly horizontal ray follows an arc of a circle of radius ρ, several times the Earth's radius R. Their ratio k = R/ρ is the refraction coefficient. Because only the difference between the two curvatures can ever be seen, the bent ray over the real Earth is equivalent to a straight ray over a larger sphere of radius R/(1 − k). With the usual k = 0.13, that is 7,323 km instead of 6,371. This is how refraction enters every calculation on a globe: the Earth gets bigger, never flat, unless k reaches 1. The drawing is schematic.
arc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a measured k of 1, which turns R/(1 − k) into an infinite radius, outside thin ducts.
snell.title: Snell's law, layer by layer
snell.mini: Air gets denser downward, so a ray going up is bent a little more level at each layer, until it levels off and comes back down. Light in air curves toward the ground, never away from it in ordinary conditions.
snell.text: The refractive index of air increases downward, with its density. A ray launched slightly upward crosses layer after layer of thinner air, and at each boundary it is bent a little more toward the horizontal, until it levels off and curves back down. The short ticks are the wavefront, always perpendicular to the ray. The dashed line is the straight chord; the real path lies above it [1]. The index steps are hugely exaggerated so the kinks are visible: in real air there are no steps, only a smooth gradient, and the broken line becomes a circular arc.
snell.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: rays in ordinary air bending as strongly as the Earth curves.
circles.title: Two circles, one subtraction
circles.mini: The Earth is one circle, the light path another, about 7.7 times larger. Below the observer's horizontal the ground falls by d²/2R and the ray by d²/2ρ. Only the gap between them can be seen.
circles.text: Two circles are enough to describe refraction over a round Earth. One is the planet, of radius R. The other is the light path, which in a uniform gradient is an arc of radius ρ = R/k, about 7.7 times larger at k = 0.13. Measured down from the observer's horizontal, the ground falls away by d²/2R over a distance d, and the ray only by d²/2ρ. Everything an observer can ever see depends on the gap between the two: refraction shrinks the effect of curvature, it never reverses it. Curvature is exaggerated by the factor printed on the image; the ratio ρ/R is exact.
circles.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a ray that falls as fast as the ground, leaving no gap to measure.
dndh.title: What bends light in air
dndh.mini: One physical quantity decides how light bends in air: how fast its refractive index falls with height. Pressure and temperature set its size; the way temperature changes with height sets its sign.
dndh.text: Refraction near the ground has one physical input: how fast the refractive index of air falls with height. The index follows density, so pressure and temperature set the size of that gradient, and the way temperature changes with height sets its sign [1]. Air cooling fast with height bends light up; air warming with height bends it down strongly. None of this is a free parameter: it follows from the measured state of the air. The profile in the drawing is illustrative, not a measured one.
dndh.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a way to make light follow the ground's curvature everywhere without the temperature profile that requires.
crossing.title: Only the gradient a ray crosses can bend it
crossing.mini: Air's index changes with height, so a ray running nearly level crosses the gradient and bends, while a steep ray hardly does. Refraction matters for distant views near the horizon, far less overhead.
crossing.text: The refractive index of air changes with height, not sideways. So only the part of the gradient a ray actually crosses can bend it. A ray running nearly level crosses it across its whole length and bends by a measurable amount; a steep ray crosses the layers quickly and hardly bends at all [1]. That is why refraction matters for long sightlines near the horizon and much less for things high in the sky. The bending is greatly exaggerated in the drawing.
crossing.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: steep and level rays bending alike, as they would have to if refraction were a general distortion.
subtract.title: Only the difference is visible
subtract.mini: Below the same horizontal line, the ground drops by one amount and the ray by a smaller one. What an observer sees is the difference. Refraction reduces it; it cannot turn it into a rise.
subtract.text: Take the observer's horizontal as the reference. Over a distance d the ground drops below it by d²/2R. A refracted ray drops too, by the smaller amount d²/2ρ. What anyone can observe is the difference between the two, d²/2R × (1 − k), which is exactly the drop over a sphere of radius R/(1 − k). In ordinary air k is a small fraction, 0.13 on average, so refraction shrinks the effect of curvature by that fraction. It cannot change its sign unless k exceeds 1. Both drops are greatly exaggerated in the drawing.
subtract.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a ray that drops as much as the ground, so the difference vanishes, over long sightlines in ordinary weather.
morph.title: Straighten the light: the gap does not move
morph.mini: Bend the whole scene until the light ray is straight: the ray unrolls from a 49,000 km arc into a line, the planet swells from 6,371 to 7,323 km, and the hidden part of the target does not move at all.
morph.text: A demonstration of the one step behind every refraction correction. The whole scene is bent by a common amount until the light comes out straight: the same curvature is subtracted from the ray and from the ground. The ray unrolls from a 49,000 km arc (k = 0.13) into a straight line; the planet swells from 6,371 km to 7,323 km. The orange bar, the part of the far target that sits below the line of sight, does not move by a single pixel, because it depends only on the difference between the two curvatures, which the subtraction leaves alone. That is why a refracted globe is simply a larger globe.
morph.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a real atmosphere in which the subtraction leaves no curvature at all, that is, k = 1.
kline.title: k crosses zero at one temperature gradient
kline.mini: k depends almost entirely on how temperature changes with height. Air cooling at 3.42 °C per 100 m bends light not at all. To make the Earth look flat, air would have to warm by 12.9 °C per 100 m, everywhere.
kline.text: The refraction coefficient k runs in a straight line with the vertical temperature gradient [1]. Pressure and temperature only tilt the line. They cannot move where it crosses zero: air cooling at 3.42 °C per 100 m, the autoconvective lapse rate, has the same density at every height and carries light in straight lines [2]. Ordinary air cools more slowly, giving k near 0.13. To reach k = 1, where the globe would look flat, the air would have to warm with height by about 12.9 °C per 100 m over the whole sightline. Real inversions reach that only in layers tens of metres thick over cold water or ice, where they produce ducts and grotesque mirages [3]. Weather balloons have measured the real profile twice a day since 1905 [4]. The line is drawn schematically.
kline.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a permanent, worldwide warming of the air with height of about 12.9 °C per 100 m. Radiosondes do not find it.
recip.title: k is measured, not assumed
recip.mini: Two stations on towers sight each other at the same moment. Each reads its zenith angle from its own vertical. The sum gives k directly, and the heights of the stations cancel out.
recip.text: Two stations sight each other at the same moment, each reading the zenith angle from its own vertical. With no refraction, the two angles would add up to 180° plus γ, the angle between the stations at the Earth's centre, 16.19′ over 30 km. Refraction bends both rays down and subtracts kγ. So the sum gives k directly: k = 1 − (sum − 180°)/γ. The heights of the stations never appear. Simultaneity matters because k swings through the day; campaigns of this kind find k from about 0.10 by day to 0.34 by night [2], and the method is how k is monitored today [1]. The arc, the towers and the bend are exaggerated in the drawing.
recip.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: simultaneous reciprocal zenith angles adding to 180° plus exactly γ, that is, k = 1.
r206.title: One road, ten sessions: near the ground, k is weather
r206.mini: A surveyor sighted between two marks 1.54 km apart on Route 206, New Jersey, ten times, both ways at once, 1.6 m above the road. The refraction coefficient k came out anywhere from −0.48 to +0.94 [1].
r206.text: Jesse Kozlowski fixed two marks 1.54 km apart on the shoulder of US Route 206 in New Jersey by GNSS, then sighted from each to the other at the same moment with total stations about 1.6 m above the road: in November 2015, on three days of November 2016, and in 2018 [1]. Each instrument reads the zenith angle from its own vertical; the instrument heights cancel in the sum, which exceeds 180° by an excess ε. The two verticals are γ = 49.9″ apart, the angle between the two GNSS positions seen from the Earth's centre: this is where the radius enters, through the satellite frame. Then k = 1 − ε/γ. The excess ranged from 3″ to 75″, so k ranged from +0.94 to −0.48 on the same line, negative through a whole November midday, when the road was warmer than the air and the light sagged toward it. The standard 0.13 is an average over many conditions, not a promise for one line at 1.6 m.
r206.verdict: On its own this line does not decide the shape, and is not offered for that: the weather moves the excess (3″ to 75″) more than the curvature does (49.9″). Would favour the flat model: an excess that stays the same on lines of several lengths instead of growing with distance; that test needs longer lines.
layer.title: When k changes with height
layer.mini: Near water, the air's temperature changes fastest in the first metres, so a ray skimming the surface bends far more than one a few metres up. The bottom of a distant object can sink or stretch while its top is drawn almost normally.
layer.text: The refraction coefficient k is set by the temperature gradient of the air the ray crosses. Well above the ground the gradient is steady and one k describes the whole path. Within a few metres of water or ground it is set by the surface: strongest at the bottom, fading roughly as the logarithm of height [1]. So rays from the same scene, seen by the same eye, cross different air. Over warmer water the low rays bend upward and the foot of a distant object sinks and is squeezed, with a mirrored strip beneath it. Over colder water the low rays are trapped, and distant things loom or stack into a Fata Morgana [1][2]. One number cannot describe such a picture, which is why sightlines that skim water are weak tests of shape either way.
layer.verdict: Layered air is the flat model's strongest version of refraction. Would favour the flat plane: feet of distant objects hidden by the amount the globe predicts, day after day, with thermometers at the water and a few metres up showing no layer at all.
caus.title: What air does each model need for a measured dip?
caus.mini: From the plateau de Caussols, {{rcH}} m above the sea, the horizon was measured {{rcDip}}′ below level. For that dip the globe needs air of about {{rcTg}} °C at the eye. The plane needs {{rcTf}} °C.
caus.text: On 13 June 2026 the sea horizon was measured {{rcDip}}′ below eye level from Caussols, {{rcH}} m above the Mediterranean. The ray that grazes the sea and reaches the eye crosses every layer in between, but in layered air only its two ends count: on a globe n·r·cos α keeps its value along the ray (Bouguer's invariant), over a plane n·cos α does [1]. So each model fixes the refractive index, hence the temperature, the air at the eye must have, given the air at the sea. That afternoon the air at the eye was {{rcTeye}} °C. The globe needs {{rcTg}} °C ({{rcGg}} K per 100 m), a little colder, which points at the camera's reading rather than the air. The plane needs {{rcTf}} °C, a mean gradient of {{rcGf}} K per 100 m, more than three times the rate at which air becomes denser at the top than at the bottom and overturns [2][3].
caus.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: air at the eye near −120 °C on a June afternoon in Provence, or any dip read with no air capable of producing it on the globe.
zen.title: 97 lines, two angles each: the effective radius, measured
zen.mini: Surveyors of the 1800s read the zenith angle from both ends of each line. Their sum always exceeds 180°, and the excess grows with the length: s/E gives a median effective radius of {{zenReff}} km.
zen.text: The US Coast and Geodetic Survey measured both zenith angles of almost every line of its transcontinental triangulation, and Charles Schott printed them station by station [1]. On a sphere the verticals at the two ends differ by s/R and refraction takes back k of it, so the excess E = ζ₁ + ζ₂ − 180° equals (s/R)(1 − k), and s/E is the effective radius R/(1 − k): two angles and a length, no radius put in. Over {{zenN}} lines measured from both ends, in Colorado, California and around Mount Hamilton, every sum exceeds 180°, the smallest excess is {{zenMinE}}″ on a {{zenMinS}} km line, and the median line gives {{zenReff}} km ({{zenReffCo}} km in dry Colorado, {{zenReffCa}} km on the California coast).
zen.verdict: On a plane both verticals are parallel: with straight light the sum is 180°, with light bent toward the ground it is less. Would favour the flat plane: sums at or below 180°, or an excess that does not grow with distance.
zenhour.title: k is weather: one line, hour by hour, 1879
zenhour.mini: Two survey parties 72 km apart, in the Sierra Nevada and its foothills, read each other's zenith angle at the same hour for fourteen days. k is {{zenNight}} at night and falls to {{zenNoon}} in the early afternoon, every day.
zenhour.text: In September and October 1879 George Davidson's parties at Round Top, 3,173 m up, and at Jackson Butte, 714 m, 72.4 km apart, observed each other simultaneously, with thermometers and barometers at both ends [1]. Every hour of every day gives one k. It is {{zenNight}} at night and {{zenNoon}} between noon and four, because the air near the warm lower slope cools faster with height by day. The k predicted from the two ends' temperatures alone follows the night value and misses the afternoon dip: the change happens near the ground at the lower end. Through all of it the sum of the two angles stays above 180° at every one of the {{zenPairsH}} hours.
zenhour.verdict: The weather moves k, not its sign. Would favour the flat plane: any hour at which the two angles add to 180° or less.
igra.title: k in the air of 2026: 300,000 radiosondes
igra.mini: Twice a day some seven hundred stations launch a balloon that measures the air's pressure and temperature. Their k in the lowest layer: median {{igDay}} by day, {{igNight}} by night. The value at which a globe looks flat, k = 1, appears in {{igGe1N}} % of night soundings.
igra.text: The refraction coefficient follows from pressure and temperature: k = 503·P/T²·(0.0342 + dT/dh). We computed it for every sounding of 2026 in NOAA's radiosonde archive [1], {{igN}} soundings from {{igSt}} stations, in the lowest layer (ground to 50–300 m) and over the first kilometre. By day the lowest layer gives a median of {{igDay}}, half the values between {{igDayQ1}} and {{igDayQ3}}: the 0.13 used for sightlines is a daytime value near the ground. By night the ground cools the air above it and the median rises to {{igNight}}. Over the first kilometre the spread is narrow, {{igKmDay}} by day and {{igKmNight}} by night. R/(1 − k) is infinite at k = 1, a ray curving exactly as the ground does: that air was found in {{igGe1N}} % of night soundings and {{igGe1D}} % of daytime ones in the lowest layer, mostly over the Antarctic plateau, and in none over the first kilometre.
igra.verdict: k is the ray's curvature divided by the Earth's, so the radius is its unit: a check, not a measurement. Would favour the flat plane: k at 1 or more in most soundings, in every climate, by day and by night.
beam.title: A laser beam is a cone, not a line
beam.mini: A hand-held laser spreads by about 1 milliradian. At 15.3 km its beam is {{lasW}} m tall, and fired level 1 m above water, its lower edge touches the water after {{lasEdge}} km.
beam.text: A laser across the sea looks like a clean test of the water's shape: fire it level from one shore and the bulge should hide it from the other. But the beam widens with distance, w = w₀ + θd: a pointer of 1 mrad is {{lasW}} m tall at 15.3 km [1]. Fired level from a height h, its lower edge reaches the water at 2h/θ, {{lasEdge}} km for 1 m. The width decides where some ray points, not whether one can get there: if the bulge is in the way, no ray of the cone reaches the eye. What lets one through is the air, a metre above water, at night.
beam.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a beam much narrower than the hidden height (a surveyor's laser at 0.1 mrad spreads 1.5 m over 15.3 km, against 10.8 m hidden) whose centre arrives at the height of a straight line over a plane, under measured air.
laser.title: Worthing–Brighton, 2019: a laser test redone in its own air
laser.mini: Laser and camera 1 m above the sea, 15.3 km apart. The globe hides the beam unless the air warms by {{lasG2}} °C over 2 m. The operators' thermometers at Worthing measured 1.5 °C; at Brighton, nothing they could resolve.
laser.text: On 23 February 2019 a group fired lasers between Worthing Pier and Brighton's West Pier, 15.3 km apart, lasers and cameras 1 m above the water, and saw the beams [1]. Without air the globe hides a 1 m laser from a 1 m eye by {{lasHid}} m; with k = 0.13, by {{lasHidK}} m. It is seen if the air bends light with a uniform k of {{lasKNeed}}: air warming by {{lasGNeed}} °C per metre at that evening's pressure. They measured the air at both ends with two thermometers good to ±0.25 °C [1][2]. At Worthing both show it warming by 1.5 °C between the water and 2 m; traced through that air ray by ray, the beam reaches the far camera on the globe directly, and on a plane only by reflection off the water. At Brighton the readings are flat within their precision, an air in which the globe hides the beam, but which cannot be told apart from the air it needs. The test measured the air, with thermometers too coarse to read it.
laser.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a narrow beam well above the water, thermometers good to 0.05 °C at both ends and halfway showing no warming with height, and the beam's centre arriving where a straight line over a plane puts it, by day and by night, in both directions. Would favour the globe: the same beam hidden by the predicted amount, with the same thermometers.
